t.2.81.1: Having heard the words of Guha, deeply unwelcome, Bharata fell into brooding thought right there, on the very spot where he had heard that unwelcome news.
t.2.81.2: Delicate yet of great strength, with shoulders like a lion's and mighty arms, with large eyes like white lotuses, youthful and pleasing to behold.
t.2.81.3: Having recovered for a brief while, he, deeply distressed in mind, suddenly fell down like an elephant pierced in the heart by goads.
t.2.81.4: Seeing Bharata in that state, Śatrughna, who stood close beside him, embraced him and wept aloud, senseless and wasted with grief.
t.2.81.5: Then all those mothers of Bharata came together, emaciated from fasting, wretched, and worn down by the calamity that had befallen their husband.
t.2.81.6: And those women, weeping, surrounded him as he lay fallen on the ground; but Kausalyā, sick at heart, went after him and embraced him.
t.2.81.7: As a loving cow embraces her own calf, the poor woman, weeping and consumed by grief, held Bharata close and questioned him.
t.2.81.8: Son, I hope no illness is afflicting your body? For today the life of this royal house depends on you.
t.2.81.9: Seeing you, my son, I live on, now that Rāma has gone away with his brother and King Daśaratha has passed away; today you alone are our protector.
t.2.81.11: Having recovered himself for a moment, that greatly renowned one, still weeping, consoled Kausalyā and spoke these words to Guha.
t.2.81.10: My son, surely you have not heard anything unpleasant about Lakṣmaṇa, have you? Or, son, about the one who has gone to the forest with his wife, the only son of me, a mother of but one son?
t.2.81.12: Where did my brother spend the night? Where was Sītā, and where Lakṣmaṇa? On what bed did he sleep, and what had he eaten? Tell me, Guha.
t.2.81.14: Food of every kind, delicacies, and fruits of many varieties, in great abundance, were brought by me for Rāma to eat.
t.2.81.13: Thus questioned, Guha, lord of the Niṣādas, told Bharata how he had conducted himself toward Rāma, his beloved and kindly guest.
t.2.81.15: Rāma, whose valour was true, courteously declined all of it; for, mindful of the duty of a warrior, he did not accept it.
t.2.81.16: "Friend, it is not for us to accept gifts; rather, we must always give." With these words, O king, that great-souled one gently won us over.
t.2.81.17: Having drunk the water brought by Lakṣmaṇa, the greatly renowned Rāghava, together with Sītā, then observed a fast.
t.2.81.18: Then Lakṣmaṇa too did the same with the water that remained, and the three of them, restrained in speech and composed in mind, performed the twilight worship.
t.2.81.19: Then afterwards Saumitri, having himself quickly brought kuśa grass, made a fine, well-spread bed for the sake of Rāghava.
t.2.81.20: Rāma lay down with Sītā upon that fine bed, and Lakṣmaṇa, having washed the feet of the two, withdrew.
t.2.81.21: This is that root of the iṅgudī tree, and this indeed is that grass on which Rāma and Sītā, both of them, lay that night.
t.2.81.22: Fastening on his back two quivers well filled with arrows, Lakṣmaṇa, the scorcher of foes, wearing his arm-guard and finger-guard and holding his great strung bow, stood all night long, keeping watch around him and nothing else.
t.2.81.23: Then I too, bearing the finest arrows and bow, took my stand there where Lakṣmaṇa was, and with my unwearying kinsmen, bows in hand, I guarded him who was like the great Indra.
